Every fact on this site is one of three kinds: A plain statement : a record shows it. “The family says” : told to us, not yet found in a record. “Probably” : it fits the records but is not proven. A few words come up often. A petition for naturalization is the form a person filed to become a United States citizen. A passenger list is the ship’s list of the people who crossed. An index line is a typed listing that points to a record but is not the record itself. Names changed shape on the way. The family name was Aoun; the family says it became Awn, and records also write it Owen and Aun. Saydah appears as Saidah and Sayda. These are the same families, and each time we say which spelling a record used. What I would love from you: corrections, names for the faces in old photographs, and the stories no record keeps. t: The Aoun (Awn) Family, from Damour to Brooklyn
x: What we found The family was Aoun in Damour. The family says the name became Awn in America, and records also wrote it Owen and Aun; Joseph’s death certificate says Owen. The Awn story begins in Damour, a coastal village south of Beirut. Damour sits on the Mediterranean coast about eleven miles south of Beirut. When the Aouns left in the summer of 1920, the First World War had only just ended, and Mount Lebanon was recovering from a wartime famine that, by most historians' estimates, killed a large share of its people. In September 1920, as the family crossed into New York State, France was proclaiming the new state of Greater Lebanon under its mandate. This is background, not a record of this family, and the papers do not tell us why Joseph and Assin decided to go. What they do tell us is that they took all eight children with them, a party of ten on third-class tickets by way of Southampton and Quebec, with Joseph about 50 years old and Brooklyn as their destination. That is a lot to stake on a new country.

Owen” was Yusuf al-Khoury Butrus Awn to his own people. Yusuf is the Arabic form of Joseph, Butrus is Peter, and the K. most likely stands for Khoury (our translation, to be confirmed by a native reader). “Death of a righteous man” Al-Hoda, 17 September 1932, p.3, the local-news headline over Joseph’s death (our translation, to be confirmed by a native reader) When Joseph died in Brooklyn on 14 September 1932, the city recorded him as “Joseph K. Owen,” retired, aged 62, the son of Peter and Teresa Owen. The Arabic paper Al-Hoda printed what looks like another man: “Yusuf al-Khoury Butrus Awn,” of Damour (our translation, to be confirmed by a native reader). He is one person, and the two names fit together. The ship list of 1920 had already written him a third way, Youseuf Aoun, a farmer of 53 (a second word is crossed out). His death certificate says he was born on 21 November 1869, and that he had lived in the United States for 12 years, which fits the family’s arrival in 1920. He died of cardiac failure with a coronary thrombosis and was buried at St. John’s Cemetery on 16 September. Al-Hoda said he died of a heart attack on the Wednesday morning, that the funeral Mass was at Our Lady of Lebanon on Hicks Street, and said that members of the Damour fraternity came (our translation). The Brooklyn Times Union says St. Mary’s Syrian Roman Catholic Church on Hicks Street; we take these to be one church under two names. The same fraternity may show up two years earlier. On the evening of Monday 28 April 1930, the Damouri Fraternity Society met at Columbus Hall and chose its officers, and its treasurer is printed as “Yusuf al-Khoury Awn” (Al-Hoda, 23 May 1930; our translation). It is probably Joseph, since the name matches the one in his notices and he was a Damour man, but nothing on the page says so, and the other Awns elected with him are named without any link to him. If it was him, he was trusted with the Damour men’s money at the age of sixty. One more page may tell us about his own family. In March 1926 the Damour magazine Ash-Shams printed a notice of the death in Brazil of “the late Jibrail,” who had emigrated about 1911, and it condoled his two brothers, “Khawaja Mikhail in Damour and Khawaja Yusuf in New York” (our translation). The notice is addressed to a Mikhail al-Khoury Boutros Awn, and Joseph’s father is Peter (Butrus) on his certificate. So Joseph may have had a brother who stayed in Damour and another who went to Brazil. This is the only record that says so, and no other record names either brother. A second Ash-Shams page, of July 1934, mentions the family of a “late Jibrail al-Khoury Awn” in Brazil, but it names none of Joseph’s family. His wife Assin Aoun was written Essine on the ship list, Aseen in the 1925 census and Affin in one 1932 notice. Her death certificate gives her father as Joseph Segan (Segen; Sajaan in Arabic) and her mother as Susanne, with a family name that reads Nahmir in a hard-to-read hand. She died on Wednesday 16 October 1935 at Bay Ridge Hospital, a widow living at 1047 75th Street, of a ruptured appendix after an emergency appendectomy. Her son John asked for the burial permit. A Mass was said for her at Our Lady of Lebanon on Friday 18 October, the day she was buried at St. John’s, and Al-Hoda called her “the late Assin Yusuf al-Khoury Awn of Damour,” which probably puts her husband’s name after hers, the usual way in these notices. Her age is 45 on the ship list, 40 in the 1925 census and 52 in the Times Union notice (the certificate’s own age is hard to read), so her birth year is unknown. Her notice reads like a map of the neighborhood. It names her children and their families, the sons of Habib Aoun (Sajaan, Khalil, Farid, Sa’id and Shaker), a widow, Sofia Ghareeb, and the Aql family. How the Habib Aoun sons were related to Joseph or Assin we do not know. The same undertaker, Jere J. Cronin, Inc., of Atlantic Avenue, handled both Joseph’s and Assin’s funerals. The cemetery’s own burial search says that in June 1961 St. John’s moved Assin and her son George from Section 20 to Section 3, Row C, the row where the same search places Joseph’s own burial, almost thirty years after his funeral. A volunteer’s Find a Grave listing, made in 2016, still shows Assin and George in Section 20 with three other Owens we do not know. Still open Joseph’s birth: the certificate’s age of 62 years, 9 months and 7 days does not fit its own birth date of 21 November 1869, which gives 62 years, 9 months and 24 days. No Damour record has turned up. Joseph’s grave: the cemetery’s search puts his 1932 burial in Section 3, Row C, Graves 39 to 42, and Find a Grave says Grave 4A. Same man, same date, two grave numbers; and the same cemetery screen also shows a removal from Section 20 on 8 June 1961, so where he lay between 1932 and 1961 is not clear. The 1961 move: why Assin and George were moved, and whether the Section 20 listing on Find a Grave is out of date, is not known. The two sons: the Al-Hoda item of 17 September 1932 says Joseph was buried beside two sons who died young. No record in hand names them. Joseph’s brothers: Mikhail and Jibrail rest on one Ash-Shams page. Assin’s parents’ names and her age are our best readings of faint writing. Family memory: why they left Damour, what the voyage was like, or what Joseph and Assin were like. If you know, please tell Sarah. Questions for the family Does anyone remember Joseph or Assin, or stories about them? Does anyone know about two children who died young and are buried with Joseph? Does anyone know why Assin and George were moved at St. John’s in 1961? Does anyone know who Mikhail and Jibrail were, or who Michal Malleut, the uncle named on the 1920 ship list, was? Who were the sons of Habib Aoun named in Assin’s notice? Does anyone remember Esther, or a letter from Lebanon? Esther, who lived in Lebanon, is named in the Arabic notices of 1930 and 1935, and in 1961 an American paper reports her death in Beirut. “informing him of the death in Beirut, Lebanon, of his sister, Mrs. Esther Ayoub” The Caravan, 2 February 1961 Joseph and Assin’s children, as the records name them, were John, Michel (Mitchell), Elias (Louis), Anthony, George, Nassib, Esther, Matilda and Theresa. Esther is not on the 1920 ship list or in the 1925 census. The English death notices of 1932 and 1935 name only Matilda and Theresa as daughters, but the Arabic notices of 1930, 1932 and 1935 list Esther first among the sisters, and in 1930 as the wife of As’ad Aoun (our translation, to be confirmed by a native reader). The Caravan of 2 February 1961 tells the rest. A cable told Mitchell Awn of the death of his sister, Mrs. Esther Ayoub, in Beirut. She was survived by four brothers (John, Mitchel, Louis and Anthony), two sisters in Brooklyn (Mrs. Matilda Gorayeb and Mrs. Theresa Koury), a son, Antoine Ayoub, with his wife and children, and two daughters in Beirut, printed as Mrs. Sira San Remi and Mrs. Mary Awn. A Mass was said for her at Our Lady of Lebanon on Sunday, 29 January 1961. The paper gives no date of death. That she is the sister the family says stayed in Lebanon is probable, and that she is the wife of As’ad Aoun is probable too, since the Caravan’s “Ayoub” fits the name Ash-Shams gives for her husband, As’ad Ayoub Aoun. Two brothers died young. Nassib’s death certificate shows “Nassib K. Owen,” a printer, single, aged 27, who died at 37 Tompkins Place on 2 October 1924 of broncho-pneumonia, with pulmonary tuberculosis contributing; his mother is written “Aseen Owen,” and he was buried at St. John’s Cemetery on 5 October. The ship list of 1920 has him as Nessil, 22, so the certificate’s age may be a year off. Al-Hoda and Mira’at al-Gharb printed his family’s notice on 3 October: he died “the evening of Thursday, the 2nd of October,” at about half past six, with prayers on Sunday at two in the afternoon at Our Lady of Lebanon, from the house on Tompkins Place (our translation, to be confirmed by a native reader). Ash-Shams of 1 November 1924 called him “lamented for his youth,” aged 27. George’s death came in the summer of 1930, and no certificate for it has been found. The family’s own notice in Mira’at al-Gharb of 30 July says he died on Sunday, 27 July, “after a sudden accident,” in a year of his age “not exceeding the twenty-fourth,” with prayers that day at Our Lady of Lebanon and the home address 466 78th Street (our translation, to be confirmed by a native reader). The Arabic papers call it a drowning: a boat that overturned, a companion who escaped with difficulty, and neither man able to swim. St. John’s Cemetery records his interment on 30 July 1930 and his move to Section 3, Row C on 8 June 1961. Two months after the drowning Ash-Shams printed his portrait. The family has told the story a little differently. The family says, through Jackie, that two of Anthony’s brothers died young: one drowned, and one died after surgery on his arm. The records bear out the drowning, but Nassib’s certificate names pneumonia and tuberculosis, not surgery, so the arm surgery does not yet match either brother. Still open Where George drowned. Mira’at al-Gharb says a canoe on a lake on Long Island, As-Sayeh the shore of Long Island, Ash-Shams a lake in Rhode Island “near New York,” and Al-Hoda a lake “about fifty miles from Brooklyn”; none is confirmed. George’s age: Ash-Shams says 22, the family’s notice “not exceeding” 24. The hour of his service, two in the afternoon in Mira’at and three in the first Al-Hoda printing, and whether he left home on Saturday or Sunday morning. Nassib’s day of death: Thursday 2 October on the certificate and the paid notices, but “last Friday” in As-Sayeh of 6 October. Which brother, if either, had the arm surgery. Esther’s birth, marriage and death dates, and her husband’s full name. All the Arabic readings are our translation, to be confirmed by a native reader. Family memory: George, Nassib or Esther. Document 112 Nassib’s border card, 3 September 1920: age 22, travelling with “Youssouf, 53,” bound for Brooklyn “c/o Aunt.” From the record; the address is our reading. 25 Aug 1920 The family leaves Southampton on the Grampian 3 Sep 1920 The ship lands at Quebec 5 Sep 1920 Most of them cross into New York State at Rouses Point Then On to Brooklyn What we found Nassib’s own border card shows where the oldest son was headed: Brooklyn, in care of an aunt, at what we read as 202 Baltic Street. The ship list names only an uncle back in Damour, so the card is the first sign of a relative on this side of the ocean (the aunt’s name is our reading of faint writing; the Quebec arrival sheet for the same party names a sister, Mrs. Owen, at 202 Baltic Street). “Uncle, Michal Malleut, Damour” The S.S. Grampian passenger list, Quebec, 3 September 1920, the nearest relative named for the whole family On 25 August 1920 the Aoun family left Southampton on the S.S. Grampian, bound for Quebec, on third-class tickets. One of the small cards from that crossing, Anthony’s identification card, is still held by the family. It carries a doctor’s vaccination stamp, the words “U.S.A. Passenger,” and a hand-written “11” after the word “line” (our reading), which would be his line on the ship’s list. On the list, which was made out for the landing at Quebec on 3 September, the family stands together on lines 5 to 14. Joseph is written Youseuf, a farmer of 53 who could read Arabic. Assin is Essine, 45, “H’wife.” After them come Thirese (14), Georges (10), Michel (8), Elias (6) and Antoine (4), and then the older three: Nessil (22), Matilde (29) and Jean (16), whose calling is written “Carpenter.” Everyone’s last home is Damour, the destination is Brooklyn, and the nearest relative named for the whole party is an uncle, Michal Malleut, in Damour. No one in America is named. The list does not say how they were related; that the nine are Joseph and Assin’s children comes from the family and from the later records. From Quebec they went on by train. The naturalization papers of Anthony, Matilda, Mitchell, Theresa and John give 5 September 1920 for crossing into New York State at Rouses Point, and several name the Delaware & Hudson Railway. Elias’s papers give 7 September. Nassib’s border card then fills in a little more. It was filed on the same day as the ship list. It repeats the head-tax number from line 12, 5586, and it calls his nearest relative “Michel Mallout” of Damour, probably the same uncle spelled another way (our reading). It also says that his passage was paid by his parents (our reading). Not everything adds up. Anthony is 4 on the list but 6 by his own birth date, 6 March 1914. A 1940 Brooklyn Eagle story says that John came with “his father, mother, two sisters and four brothers,” but the list shows two sisters and five brothers besides John. The count of four does not match the list, and why is not known. Still open The uncle: Michal Malleut is named for the whole family, and “Michel Mallout” on Nassib’s card is probably the same man. No record says who he was. The aunt: Nassib’s card says “c/o Aunt” and a name we cannot read, at an address we read as 202 Baltic Street, Brooklyn; the Quebec arrival sheet names “Sister, Mrs. … Owen, 202, Baltic Street.” The 1920 census page for that house lists an Owen household there; that it is the same family is a lead, not proven. The ages: six of the nine children’s ages on the ship list do not match the 1925 census. Matilda is 29 on the list, 23 in the census, and born in 1899 by her own petition, so 20 on the ship. How many came: the Eagle’s count of four brothers against the list’s five. The day at Rouses Point: 5 September in five of the family’s papers, 7 September in Elias’s. Family memory: why they left Damour, what they carried, who met them in Brooklyn. If you know, please tell Sarah. Questions for the family Does anyone know who Michal Malleut, the uncle, was? Does anyone know who the aunt on Baltic Street was? Did anyone hear why the family left Damour in 1920, or what the trip was like? An index line, which points to the record but is not the record. Its “Brooklyn” as a birthplace is most likely the destination column misread. Nassib, who had died at the same address the October before, is correctly left off the page. “Still Aid in Fight for Success, He Tells 173 Graduates at Hamilton” Brooklyn Daily Eagle, 30 June 1932, page 16 By 1925 the family lived at 37 Tompkins Place in Brooklyn. x: Helen's father, Antoon (W.) Saydah , came from Forzul , Lebanon. We call him Antoon, which is how the Arabic papers and his 1942 draft card write his first name; many records write it Anton, and some Antoun. His family name appears as Saydah, Saidah, Sayda, Saida and even Smyda. Helen's mother was born a Hadad (Wassela Hadad), a name that records also spell Hodod, Haddad and Hadel.

It is on his declaration of 1909 and again on his passport application of 1923 (as printed: “tatoo cross on left hand”). “tattoo cross (x) on left hand” Antoon’s declaration of intention, no. 9718, 9 November 1909 On 9 November 1909, in the Supreme Court of Kings County, a merchant named Antoon Wahbeh Saydah described himself for the clerk. He was 28, white, with a dark complexion, five feet six and 170 pounds, with black hair and brown eyes, and “tattoo cross (x) on left hand.” He lived at 570 48th Street, and he signed with an x before his name. In December 1923 he described himself again for a passport clerk, and the cross was still there. By those same sworn papers he was born in Forzul on 15 August 1881 and left Le Havre on the liner La Touraine about 17 October 1898, reaching New York on 25 October. We have not found his name on that sailing. The one line that may be him is on a La Touraine list marked as arriving on 28 November 1898: “Smyda, Antoun,” 18, single, a farmer who could read, from Beyrouth, with $20 and a “Brother, 73 W’g’ton St.” as his destination. A month apart and a spelling apart, it is not proven, and we treat it as a question for the family. If it is him, the brother is probably Khaleel, who lived at 73 Washington Street in 1900. The 1900 census finds an Anton Saydah, born 15 August 1880, aged 19 and single, a boarder in Abdalla Kirkish’s household in Negaunee, Michigan, “selling goods from house to house.” The Kirkish wife, Sady, is probably his sister Sada. By April 1910 he was back in Brooklyn, a single man of 29 in his brother Khaleel’s household at 570 48th Street, which is what proves that the two were brothers. His citizenship papers run from 1909 to 1914. On 8 May 1913 he petitioned as a merchant living at 5305 Sixth Avenue with his wife, Wassila. Two witnesses swore that they had known him in New York State since December 1905: Anton Simon, a commission merchant, and Willard Van Wagner, in dry goods. The petition also says “I have no children.” Their daughter Lily had been born and had died in March 1913, two months before, and we read the line as meaning living children. On 22 January 1914 he took the oath in open court, renouncing the Sultan of Turkey, and was handed certificate no. 381478, with the last digit written over. Written under it is a new address, 4721 Sixth Avenue. The directories and cards that follow show a working man. The 1913 Brooklyn directory lists him as “laces,” at 567 48th Street, the house where Khaleel, an importer, is listed too. On the draft card he signed on 12 September 1918 he is a manager at the Saydah Importer Co., 85 Washington Street, and his wife Wassela is his nearest relative. That card gives his birth as 15 August 1880, a year earlier than his own citizenship papers. In December 1923 he applied for a passport “for buying and manufacturing merchandise” for the Saydah Importing Co. across a long list of countries, from Portugal and Madeira to Egypt, Syria and Switzerland, naming his father, Wahbeh A. Saydah, as dead. His photograph is attached to it; he was 42. He sailed on the Lapland on 16 January 1924 for about a year. The passenger lists let us follow part of the trip. On 11 July 1924 he was in Southampton as a first-class passenger on the Arundel Castle, with Madeira as the likely port of call (our reading of an abbreviation). On 4 August a first-class passenger named “Anton Wahlbeh Saydah,” 42, a U.S. merchant, came back to Southampton from a port we read as Madeira on the Kildonan Castle; this is probably him. On 12 August he landed in New York from the Majestic, giving his home as 33 86th Street, Brooklyn. He had been gone about seven months, not a year. His name is also on the 1924 Brooklyn voter list, at 33 86th Street. The last of his own papers is the draft card of 1942, the “old man’s” registration for men born between 1877 and 1897. He was 61 by its count, living at 33 86th Street and still working for the Saydah Importing Co., at 236 Fifth Avenue. His wife “Wassella” is the person who will always know his address. He signed in English letters, with a handwritten note under the signature line that reads, as we read it, “arabic signature.” The back describes a man of five feet five and 180 pounds. Still open His birth year: his sworn papers of 1909, 1913 and 1923 say 15 August 1881. The 1900 census, his 1918 draft card and his passenger list age of 18 say 1880. The 1942 card writes 1881 but gives an age of 61, which fits 1880. The day, 15 August, is the same in every record. His arrival: 25 October 1898 on his own papers, about September 1898 from Beirut on his passport application, 1900 on the 1930 census, and about 1901 on others. No Ellis Island search has found him, and the La Touraine line of 28 November is only a possible match. A baptism record from Forzul might settle this and his birth year. His certificate: certificate no. 381478 on his own papers, but the handwritten number 423396 beside his name on the 1924 Majestic list is unexplained. Forzul or Forgul: the cursive letter in his birthplace is not settled. Family memory: stories of the voyage, why he left, the cross on his hand, or the trip to Madeira. If you know, please tell Sarah. Questions for the family Does anyone know what took Antoon to Michigan, or who met him in New York? Did anyone hear stories of his voyage in 1898, or about the cross on his hand? What did he buy on the 1924 trip, and did he talk about Madeira? Saydah, 31, of 567 48th st” and “Wassela Hadad, 23,” of Henry Street (the house number is blurred in print; the certificate has 301). Four days before the wedding, Mira’at al-Gharb printed the invitation. The paper had received word of the wedding of “Antoun Effendi Sayyida” and “Miss Wasila, daughter of Khawaja Hanna al-Haddad,” at 3:30 on “Sunday next” in the Episcopal Trinity Church at the corner of Montague and Clinton streets (our translation, to be confirmed by a native reader). The certificate gives her father as John. We take Hanna and John to be one name, but that is not proven. They were married on Sunday, 5 May 1912, at the Church of the Holy Trinity in Brooklyn. The certificate says Antoon, 31, a merchant of 567 48th Street, was born in “Furzol, Syria,” and that Wassela, 23, of 301 Henry Street, was born in “Zahleh.” His parents are written “Wahbah Saydah” and “Noor Jereisaty” (our reading), hers “John Hodod” and “Amina Shehadi.” It was the first marriage for both. Their witnesses were “Maheeba Fuleihan” (as we read it) and Antoon’s brother Khaleel, and the Bureau of Records stamped the paper received nine days later, on 14 May. A cousin of Antoon’s, Michael Butrus Kirkish of Ishpeming, Michigan, sent his congratulations to the Arabic paper Jurab al-Kurdy on 9 May (the date is the archive’s; the page prints none; our reading of the signature and translation); how the Kirkish family was related is a question for the family. Their first child, Lily, was born on 5 March 1913 and lived three days. Her death certificate gives the address 5305 Sixth Avenue, where the family lived that spring, and says she was born between the sixth and seventh month and died of atelectasis, the lungs not having fully opened. The physician is written “R. G. Haddad,” of 56 Garden Place. Lily was buried at Mount Olivet Cemetery on 10 March 1913. The censuses then follow the household. In June 1915 the state census has “Saydah, Anton,” 36, a cotton goods converter, with his wife Wassela, 26. In January 1920 they are counted with Helen, almost three. By June 1925 the household at 33 86th Street has three daughters, Helen, Evelyn and Virginia, and by April 1930 it is a house they own, with Antoon an importer of linen. In 1940 he is still a store owner in “imported linens,” with Wassela and Helen, 22, at home. In 1916 Antoon sold property to a buyer named Ellen Irwin, as a line in the Kings County deed index shows; the index points to the deed, which we have not yet seen. Wassela outlived Antoon by almost twenty years. We hold no certificate for her death, only index lines. A newspaper index lists her obituary in The Record of Hackensack on 8 January 1969, and the New Jersey death index gives 6 January 1969 at Englewood; the Social Security index says December 1968. We do not yet know why Syracuse. “father of the virtuous lady, wife of Anton Effendi Saydah” Mira’at al-Gharb, 14 October 1913, p.2, on the death of Hanna al-Haddad (our translation, to be confirmed by a native reader) Wassela’s parents were Hanna and Amina. Her marriage certificate gives them as “John Hodod” and “Amina Shehadi,” while the Arabic papers call him “Hanna al-Haddad” of Mu’allaqa, Zahle, which is the way we take Hanna and John to be one name. The 1900 census gives his birth as March 1850 and says he had been out of work for twelve months; in 1910 he is 65. Amina appears as “Emmel” in 1900, born June 1865, with eight children born and five living, and as “Ameeny,” 45, in 1910. The censuses give 1892 as the year they arrived. In 1900 the family was living on DeGraw Street in Brooklyn, in the household of “Shehady, Beshara,” an importer born in March 1870. The census calls Amina his sister and John his brother-in-law, which is the first place we see her family name. With them are “Salem,” 16, a salesman; “Halen,” 12; “Wassilla,” 14, a saleswoman; and “Najeeb,” born in New York in October 1896. By 1910 the household is “John 65, Ameeny 45, Salim 24, Wassela 20, Charles 18 and Najib 13.” A New York City births index line gives a “Nageeb Hadded,” born 13 October 1896 to “John Hadded” and “Ameene Shadey Hadded,” which probably is Najib; the index points to the certificate, which we have not seen. A grocer named “John” appears in an 1898 Brooklyn directory at 77 Washington Street. Whether he is Wassela’s father is a question for the family. The family’s losses show up in the papers. A death certificate for “Helen Hadad,” aged three, records that she died on 21 April 1908 of diphtheria croup in the Kingston Avenue hospital, and gives her father as “John Hadad” and her mother’s maiden name as “Emmenie Shehad.” She was buried at Mount Olivet Cemetery on 23 April. She is probably Wassela’s little sister, and a ninth child fits the census counts. The Arabic paper Al-Kalemat reported on 1 May 1908 the death of “Helena, aged two, daughter of Hanna al-Haddad of Mu’allaqa, Zahle” (our translation, to be confirmed by a native reader). The Arabic page prints “12 April” for the funeral prayer, which is not the 21 April of the certificate. Wassela’s own daughter Helen, born in 1917, may have been named for her. In November 1911 the Arabic paper Mira’at al-Gharb said that a church choir would meet at the home of “Khawaja Hanna al-Haddad, No. 301 Henry Street, Brooklyn” (our translation, to be confirmed by a native reader). The marriage certificate of the next May gives 301 Henry Street as Wassela’s address, so this is probably her father’s house. On New Year’s night 1913, a “Salim Hadad, 26 years old, of 104 Atlantic avenue,” was shot in the left shoulder at the corner of Atlantic Avenue and Henry Street after a quarrel, was treated and sent home, and the other man was locked up. The Arabic paper As-Sayeh tells it as a quarrel in his shop. That he is Wassela’s brother is probable, since Henry Street fits; the paper makes him 26, the 1910 census points to 26 or 27 and the 1900 census to 28 or 29. That October, Hanna died. The Syracuse Post-Standard of 13 October 1913 reports that “John Hadad,” 68, of Brooklyn, “a brother-in-law of Michel and Joseph Shehadi of this city,” died on Saturday at Clifton Springs, where he had been for his health for eighteen months, and that the funeral would be that afternoon at the Church of the Savior in Syracuse. The Arabic papers agree on the place and the funeral. Mira’at al-Gharb of 14 October names his son-in-law as Anton Effendi Saydah, Al-Hoda of 17 October names “his son-in-law Antun Effendi Sayyida,” and the notice of 18 October counts among the mourners his widow and his sons “Salim, Khalil and Najib” (our translation, to be confirmed by a native reader). The Shehadis were two Syracuse merchants. The two Arabic notices disagree on whether they were his brothers-in-law or his “cousins,” and we lean toward brothers-in-law, so that they would be Amina’s brothers. The Shehadi newspapers and censuses we hold are on the Documents page. The records place his death on Saturday, 11 October 1913. A New York State death index line for “John Hadad” has that date, with the place “Willard” instead of Clifton Springs, and Find a Grave has a memorial for a John Hadad at Oakwood Cemetery in Syracuse, in a plot with no grave marker. Both are leads to a record rather than the record itself. Still open Where Hanna died and where he lies. The papers say Clifton Springs, the death index says “Willard,” the Post-Standard names a cemetery of which only “Mornin…” can be read in our copy, and Find a Grave says Oakwood. Hanna’s death certificate, number 50442, may settle it. How long Hanna was at Clifton Springs: eighteen months by the Post-Standard, eight months by the Arabic letter of 18 October. How the Shehadis were related to Hanna: brothers-in-law in two notices, “cousins” in the third. Which son-in-law the Arabic letter of 18 October means by “Amin Sayda,” and who “Khalil” was, since no census lists a son by that name. Salim’s age, 26 in the paper, 26 or 27 in the 1910 census and 28 or 29 in the 1900 census, and the date of the funeral prayer for little Helen. Whether the 1898 ship card for “Wassilah Hadad” is Wassela, or another girl. It says Tripoli, not Zahle, and the censuses put the family here since 1892. Whether the Najib Haddad who died in Watertown in July 1955 and is buried at Oakwood in Syracuse is Wassela’s brother, which is only probable, since his birth date differs from the index and the 1900 census. Family memory: Hanna and Amina, Salim, Charles and Najib, or why Hanna was buried in Syracuse. If you know, please tell Sarah. Questions for the family Does anyone know why Hanna was buried in Syracuse and not in Brooklyn? What became of Wassela’s brothers, and who was Khalil? Was Wassela’s daughter Helen named for the little girl who died in 1908? Do you know whether Hanna ran a grocery on Washington Street? On Tuesday 5 September 1916 a car on the way back to Brooklyn from Milford, Pennsylvania, overturned near Tuxedo Park, New York. Najib S. Maloof, of 4616 Sixth Avenue, who had been riding with friends, was thrown out and died of his injuries; the Daily Times says about an hour later in Tuxedo Hospital, and the Eagle’s 1918 report says he was “instantly killed.” The papers do not agree on whose car it was or who was driving. The Arabic papers do not agree among themselves: Mira’at al-Gharb calls it Antoon’s car, Al-Hoda says it was Antoon’s car with Khaleel driving, and As-Sayeh calls it “the car of Khalil Saydah” (our translations, to be confirmed by a native reader), while the Eagle’s 1918 report has Antoon “at the wheel.” That the “Khalil Saydah” of one Arabic paper is our Khaleel is probable, not proven. Maloof’s widow, Affife, asked the Kings County Surrogate’s Court on 11 September 1916 for letters of administration; the petition names three minor children and a cause of action against “Anton Saydah” for damages. On 24 June 1918 a jury before Justice Cropsey awarded her $17,500 against Antoon. The Appellate Division reversed the verdict and ordered a new trial on 14 December 1918, a request for reargument was denied on 11 January 1919, and the case appears on the court calendar for 20 January 1919. After that we have found nothing, and the Arabic papers of 1916 to 1919 do not report the trial. Maloof’s funeral was held from his home with special services, and he is on a Find a Grave listing at Green-Wood Cemetery (a lead, not proof). A boarder called “Maloof, Nazeeb” lived with Khaleel in Manhattan in the 1900 census; he is probably the same man, but that is not proven. Still open Whose car it was, who was driving, and who else was hurt: the accounts disagree. Maloof’s age: 52 in both English papers, 51 in the Arabic notice, 50 by Find a Grave. How the lawsuit ended after January 1919. We have not seen a court file past the 1916 petition. Family memory: has anyone heard this story? If you know, please tell Sarah. In his own typed letter of 1915 he says that he came to America at fourteen and “have not crossed the ocean since.” His passport applications put his sailing in the autumn of 1891: about 1 October on the 1922 application, about 10 October on the 1915 one, and about 25 September on the 1919 one. His first sure trace in Chicago is a directory of 1904, which lists “Saydah Michael W.” at 370 31st Street, and an office directory of 1907 lists “Saydah M W, oriental gods” in room 404 of the Star Building on Dearborn Street. A Cook County death index line gives a Samura Saydah, born 11 December 1911 and died 13 April 1912, probably Michael’s daughter. He swore on 30 November 1915 in Chicago that he had been naturalized by the Cook County Circuit Court on 18 March 1903. That is his own statement; we have not seen the certificate. A passport came on 3 December 1915, and on 22 January 1916 he left for Funchal, on the island of Madeira, “for the purpose of Manufacturing Embroideries,” while Zakeya and the boys stayed in Chicago. Victor, born 15 December 1918, died on 31 December 1919 at 570 48th Street of bronchial pneumonia, and Theodore died on 9 February 1922 at 8726 Fort Hamilton Parkway, aged eleven months, of encephalitis, and was buried at Mount Olivet. From the record. 1900 A jeweler at Deep River, Iowa, probably Murad 26 Jul 1904 Patent for a watch-repair tool May 1910 A patient named Murad Sayyidah, 39, at a Cook County hospital (probably him) 2 Jan 1920 Murad is counted at home in Oak Park, Illinois 6 Jan 1920 An inmate named Murad Sayyidah, 48, at the Chicago State Hospital for the Insane (an open question) 29 May 1920 Nora, his daughter, dies 18 Dec 1926 His son Fares marries Alice Awad 7 Sep 1929 Tirkman dies, “widow of Murad Saydah” What we found The brother we know least turns out to have been an inventor. In July 1904 a Murad W. Sayyidah of Deep River, Iowa, was granted a patent for a tool for repairing watches. The patent is printed in the record; that he is Antoon’s brother is probable, because the name, the town, the jeweler’s trade and the family all fit. “a new and Improved Combination-Tool for Watch-Repair” U.S. patent no. 766,067, 26 July 1904, by Murad W. Sayyidah of Deepriver, Iowa In the summer of 1904, a jeweler in Deep River, Iowa, put his name to an invention. “Murad W. Sayyidah,” a citizen of the United States, described a combination tool for watch repair, and the Patent Office granted it on 26 July. We hold the patent itself. The same spelling, Sayyidah, is on an 1895 naturalization index card for a Murad W. Sayyidah in Cook County, Illinois, whose witness was a Khaleel Sayyidah (an index card points to the record but is not the record). The 1900 census at Deep River lists a jeweler written “William Sayydah” with a wife, Mary, and sons Ferris and Harold, and Cecil’s delayed birth certificate of 1940 calls his father Murad a “watch maker” at Deep River in 1901. We think these are all one man, Antoon’s brother Murad. The name, the town, the trade and the family all fit, but no record says it in so many words. Murad was alive in January 1920. That month’s census finds him in Oak Park, Illinois, head of the household, in the “jewelry” trade with his “own store.” Tirkman heads her own household in the 1925 census with no husband in the house, and she is a widow by 1929; we do not know when or where he died. What the records show is his widow, Tirkman (her family name appears as Abu Ayn in an Arabic paper, probably; our translation, to be confirmed by a native reader), and her children Fares (written Ferris on his marriage certificate), Harold and Cecil, and Nora, who died in 1920. Nora’s death certificate of 29 May 1920 names her father as Murad Saydah. In 1926 a Mrs. Tirkman Sayda (probably Tirkman) gave to the Zahle Relief Committee, a fund for the homeland, and in May 1927 an Arabic paper listed a Mrs. Tirkman Saydah among the Syrian women sailing to Lebanon that week. It is probably Tirkman, but whether she went, and who went with her, is not shown. Then the records turn. Four days after the Oak Park census taker counted Murad at home, a census taker at the Chicago State Hospital for the Insane at Norwood Park, Illinois, wrote down an inmate named “Sayyidah Murad,” male, 48, married, born in Syria, with no occupation. That is the page as printed, dated 6 January 1920. Ten years earlier, on 4 May 1910, a “Patient” named “Sayyidah Murad,” 39, born in Syria and in the United States since 1890, was listed at the Cook County Hospital for Insane at the same place. The name, Syria and the age (within a year) fit our Murad, and 1890 is the arrival year Harold gave in 1921, though other records give other years. We do not know what to make of the January 1920 pair. It may be two men, one man counted twice (at home by his family and in the hospital), or one entry put in the wrong place, and we have not settled it. If Murad was a patient, the hospital’s own admission, discharge or death registers might say when and where he died, and we have not yet found them. Tirkman died on Saturday 7 September 1929, aged 51, at St. Mary’s Hospital in Brooklyn. Al-Hoda of 9 September, the Brooklyn Daily Times of 10 September and her death certificate call her the widow of Murad Saydah. Two families from two Lebanese villages came together in Brooklyn at the end of 1940. They did not have far to go to find each other. The Awn brothers lived at 1047 Bay Ridge Parkway, which is 75th Street, and the Saydahs at 33 86th Street, about eleven blocks away in the same Brooklyn neighborhood of Bay Ridge. We do not yet know how Anthony and Helen met, and it is a good question for the family.

Awn was born in Damour on 6 March 1914 and says he came in at Rouses Point, New York, on 5 September 1920 as “Antoine Aoun,” by train from Quebec. When he filed his declaration of intention on 4 May 1939 he was 25, single and living at 1047 Bay Ridge Parkway, and he called himself a “negligee salesman.” He described himself as dark-complexioned, with brown eyes and dark brown hair, gave his race and nationality as Syrian, and signed “Anthony Aoun.” His draft card of 16 October 1940 names his employer as “Koury-Awn’ Inc.” at 38 East 32nd Street and gives his brother John at 1047 Bay Ridge Parkway as the person to contact. It also gives his country of citizenship as “France,” which probably reflects Lebanon’s status under the French Mandate, though no record says so. His address was changed by hand to a Marine Avenue number. We do not know who owned Koury-Awn, Inc.; it may have been a business of his brother-in-law Michael Koury, but that is only a guess. Mitchell’s card, written the same day, names a different employer, John Aoun at 82 Greenwich Street, so Anthony’s East 32nd Street employer was not John’s business at that address. He took the oath of citizenship on 10 November 1942. His petition calls him “Anthony Aoun, also Anthony Joseph Awn,” a clerk at 123 Marine Avenue, married to Helen (born 9 January 1917 in Brooklyn), with a son, Joseph, born 14 November 1941, and asks that his name become Anthony Awn. It gives the marriage date as 29 December 1940; the wedding section has the dates that disagree. His witnesses, Louis Glayat and Jerome Kinberg, both salesmen, swore they had known him since 1 January 1933. By 1946 a shop called Awn’s Specialty Shop, at 82 Greenwich Street near Rector Street in Lower Manhattan, was advertising for a salesgirl in lingerie and sportswear, and it kept advertising in 1949, 1965 and 1984. The 1950 census calls Anthony a “comptroller” in retail ladies’ wear, and his 1966 obituary calls him an associate in the shop. The family says the brothers began with a fabric store and that Anthony, John, Elias, Theresa and Matilda all worked in the business (the family’s account). He was also active in the community. The Caravan, the Lebanese-American newspaper, lists a “Mitchell Awn” and an “Anthony Awn” among the officers of the St. Nicholas Young Men’s Club in 1953 and 1954, and pictures him as its president in November 1955, with a re-election notice in February 1956. His 1966 obituary calls him a past president of the St. Nicholas Young Men’s Association, which fits the 1955 and 1956 items that name him beside his photograph as president; that the 1953 and 1954 officers are our Mitchell and Anthony is probable. A “Tony Awn” won the Class B golf championship at the Syramar Golf Club in 1963, probably him. The family belonged to Our Lady of Lebanon, the Maronite church in Brooklyn Heights, where the family’s funerals were held in the 1920s and 1930s when it stood at 295 Hicks Street; Joseph’s wedding there in 1967 is on record. Part of good research is knowing which records are not ours. These are written down so nobody has to search for them twice. Joseph Owen, who died 27 April 1932 at 385 Clinton Street, is not Anthony's father. His death certificate (no. 9788) calls him a grocer of 55 whose wife was Sadie and whose parents were Michael and Mary, and says he had lived in the U.S. 18 years. Joseph (Anthony's father) died in September 1932, aged 62, married to Assin, with parents Peter and Teresa. The same cemetery (St. John's) and the same undertaker (Jere J. Cronin, Inc.) buried both, but Owen was a common spelling among Brooklyn Syrian families and nothing ties the two men together (a different man, since the ages, wives, parents and addresses differ). A "John Khouri" fruit-store lead is not John Awn (Family, from Sarah). A 1906 petition by a Salim Haddad (born 1883, in the U.S. since 1900, living on Washington Street in Manhattan) and a 1897 Kansas City card for a Salim Hadad are probably different men from Wassela's brother Salim, who was in Brooklyn by 1892 and in the June 1900 census. The January 1898 ship card for ten-year-old "Wassilah Hadad" Probably describes a different girl, because the Hadads were already living in Brooklyn. The 1920 Ishpeming census page for an Assad Kirkish household (pictured in Document 106) is probably a different Kirkish family. Assad's wife Sadie (born an Abraham, by her Social Security line) is probably not Antoon’s sister Sa’da; the Sada of the 1899 Negaunee birth return and the 1920 Munising census, wife of Abdalla Kirkish, probably is. George Abraham Saydah of Bay Ridge is not shown to be related. His 1923 declaration says he was born on 15 October 1880 (his 1926 petition says 1882), sailed from Naples on the Prinzess Irene and reached New York on 29 or 30 August 1906 (last foreign residence Cairo), and lived on Ovington Avenue in Brooklyn, with wife Melia and three children born in Hoboken. His petition number is 68097. Nothing in the papers names Antoon, Khaleel or Michael, so he stays here until a record links him (a link is only a question for the family; FamilySearch, Brooklyn naturalizations, National Archives image group 007784999, images 703, 705 and 706 of 1018). Antone Saddy, a 22-year-old Syrian lodger in the 1920 Manhattan census (sheet 10A, census district 1421; FamilySearch record 3:1:33SQ-GRNV-WRQ, image 1127 of 1176) is probably a different man, since Antoon Saydah was in Brooklyn with his wife and daughter in January 1920. “Ambassador George Hakim,” Lebanon’s representative to the United Nations, on the front page of The Caravan, 22 June 1961, is probably not George Michael Hakim, the husband of Virginia. Virginia's husband George was a Brooklyn man, a Columbia graduate and an Army staff sergeant in 1945, and later a marketing executive in New Jersey. Nothing on the page mentions Brooklyn or the Saydah or Awn families, and Hakim is a common Lebanese name (Brooklyn Newsstand, Caravan, 22 June 1961, page 1). A Social Security index line for “V Hakim,” born 1925 and died 2006, last living in New York, is not Virginia Saydah Hakim. Her obituary says she was born in 1921 and died on 26 August 2015, which is after that index line’s date and does not match it (Social Security Death Index; obituary in The Record, 27 August 2015).

A family history is never finished. These are the open questions, grouped by family line. Each says what is open and which record would settle it. If you know anything about any of them, please use the sharing form below. The Aoun (Awn) family The wedding of Anthony and Helen. Two Arabic papers and Anthony’s petition give Sunday 29 December 1940; a Caravan anniversary note of 1958 gives 28 December. We hold only an index line for the marriage license. The license itself, or the 1940 registers of St. Anselm’s or Our Lady of Lebanon, would settle the date and the church. Anthony’s death. His obituary says he died suddenly on 6 July 1966; a memorial page gives 9 July, which may be the burial day. We do not have his death certificate or the cemetery’s burial record, and the Daily News notice of 8 July 1966 is known only from an index line. Anthony’s country on paper. Records call him “Syrian”, “Syria” and, on his 1940 draft card, “France”. No record says why. The house on 86th Street. Most records say number 95; one 1958 notice says 96. It is probably a misprint, but we have not shown it. The 1947 deed that is probably Anthony’s purchase of the house has not been requested. The family in 1930. We have not found the Awn family’s 1930 census page. Helen’s later addresses. An index of public records gives Helen addresses after her death in 2000. We treat index lines as pointers, and the certificate and memorial card agree on 26 January 2000. Small age differences. Anthony’s age on the 1950 census (35, where his birth date gives 36) and Helen’s on the 1940 census (22, where hers gives 23) are each one year off. Helen’s own records. Her birth certificate or baptism, her 1976 marriage license to Gilbert Zaloom (only an index line), and her death certificate of January 2000 are not yet in hand. A family member can ask for the death certificate. For Gilbert we would also like his 1940 census page, draft card, army enlistment and Saint John burial record (1995), and the Caravan of 21 May 1959, which an index says reported his marriage to a Helen Batrouney. The five children. We have no birth or baptism records for them, and only one marriage license (an index line). A 1951 Arabic paper calls a baby girl “the third child” when four had been born: a miscount, or “third daughter”? A question for the family. Awn’s Specialty Shop and Koury-Awn, Inc. The first advertisement we found is 29 October 1946 and the last 15 June 1984; we do not know when the shop opened or closed. We would like to know who ran Koury-Awn, Inc. (Anthony’s employer in 1940, at 38 East 32nd Street). 82 Greenwich Street was John’s business address on his draft cards before the shop ads; who ran that business is not known. Photographs of the shop would help. Joseph and Assin in Lebanon. We have found no church or civil records from Damour. Parish and civil registers there could take us back past Joseph. Joseph’s grave and age. His 1932 certificate prints a birth date of 21 November 1869, but its age of 62 years, 9 months and 7 days fits about 7 December 1869. Find a Grave and the cemetery’s own search give different grave numbers for him in Section 3, Row C. Saint John’s full records, including why Joseph, Assin and George were moved in June 1961, have not been requested. Michal Malleut. The 1920 passenger list names “Uncle, Michal Malleut, Damour”, and Nassib’s border card names him as nearest relative. Neither says who he was. A question for the family. The children’s ages. The 1925 census ages for six of the nine children (Aseen, George, Michael, Elias, Matilda and Anthony) do not match the 1920 passenger list plus five years. Matilda’s age is given as 29 in 1920, 23 in 1925, and by her petition’s birth date of 16 October 1899 would be 20 or 21 in 1920. The Eagle of 5 December 1940 also says John came with four brothers, where the list shows five (Nassib’s death in 1924 may explain it, but this is a guess). A question for the family. John’s and Theresa’s birth dates. John’s papers give 15 August 1905, 15 August 1904, 4 August 1903 and 15 August 1903. The court’s decision on his birth date has not been found; it would be in the Kings County court or naturalization file for his petition. His earlier declaration of 1926 and Theresa’s second alien registration card have not been asked for. Elias’s arrival. His papers give his entry at Rouses Point as 7 September 1920; the others’ papers give 5 September. The family says he was held back by an eye infection. No record in hand shows an infection. The Baltic Street household. In 1920, Sammel (Selim) Owen’s household was at 202 Baltic Street. The census page reads his wife’s first name as Hedda or Fedda; the family’s email says Freda. We would like to know how the family was related to them, and the Quebec sheet names only “Mrs. Owen”. Fred Gorayeb and Matilda. Fred’s birth is given as 17 December 1889, 2 October 1889, 5 November 1889 and 17 October 1890, and his arrival as 1902 and 1903. We have found nothing on his death, or where he and Matilda are buried. An index line says Matilda probably died in December 1984. When and where Theresa died. The obituary indexes point to newspaper clippings we have not read. Elias, Isabel and Hicks Street. Isabel’s 1937 marriage certificate prints her parents as Fred and Sarah Ganimy; Paterson, New Jersey records may say more about them. Anthony’s school years. A 1932 Hamilton High School class list or yearbook would show whether the “Anthony Aoun” in the Eagle is our Anthony. Brooklyn city directories for 37 Tompkins Place, 1925 to 1932, have not been searched. George Awn. He drowned on Sunday 27 July 1930. The Arabic papers disagree on where: Long Island (a canoe on a lake, or the shore), a lake in Rhode Island, or a lake about fifty miles from Brooklyn. They also differ on when he left home (Saturday, or Sunday morning after Mass), the hour of the service (two or three in the afternoon), and who the friend was. His age is given as 20 (1920 list), 23 (1925 census), 22 and about 24 (the notices). A New York death record, the New York papers of 28 and 29 July 1930, or a native Arabic reader for the notices would help. Nassib’s death. His certificate and three paid notices say Thursday evening, 2 October 1924; one Arabic paper says “last Friday”. Which brother had the arm surgery in the family story is not known (Nassib’s certificate names pneumonia and tuberculosis). Mitchell’s marriages. Mitchell married his first wife on 14 October 1940 (Yonkers, by his petition) and later Laurdes Nassr (a family tree says 1947). We do not know when the second marriage took place or how the first ended. His 1947 deed has not been read. Paul Awn’s father. A 1976 column says “whose father Louis”; Find a Grave gives Mitchell J. Awn. There may be two men named Paul Awn. He is not a child of Anthony and Helen. Joseph A. Awn’s death date. The family’s memorial card says 18 January 1989; Find a Grave gives 20 January. The cemetery’s burial record and a January 1989 death notice would settle it. Esther Ayoub’s family in Beirut. The 1961 Caravan notice names her son and two daughters in Beirut. It names no husband; Arabic papers of 1930 name As’ad Aoun as Esther’s husband (our translation). We do not have her birth, marriage or the date of her death in January 1961. Does anyone remember them? The Saydah family Antoon’s birth year. His own papers say 15 August 1881; the 1900 census and his ship’s age of 18 fit 1880; one 1915 age points to 1878 or 1879. A Forzul baptism record would settle it, but we have found none. Antoon’s ship and arrival. He swore he arrived on La Touraine on 25 October 1898. The only matching entry, “Antoun Smyda,” 18, is on a list dated 28 November 1898 and may not be him. Several records give about 1900 or 1901 instead, though the 1900 census and his 1923 passport application say 1898. We need the 25 October sailing’s page, or a record that rules the Smyda entry in or out. 73 Washington Street, 1898. The La Touraine entry says he was joining a brother at 73 Washington Street. That is probably Khaleel, but we have not shown where Khaleel lived in 1898. A grocer named John Haddad is listed at 73 Washington Street in an 1898 Brooklyn directory, which looks like a coincidence of number only. Antoon’s naturalization. His petition shows a certificate number of 381478, issued 22 January 1914, with the last digit written over; a handwritten number beside his name on the 1924 Majestic list is different. The certificate itself has not been seen. Wassela’s birth year and birthplace. The 1900 census says May 1886; later records fit about 1889 to 1893 (the Social Security index says 20 December 1889). Is Zahleh really her birthplace? Her 1969 death certificate may give a date; we do not have it, only a newspaper index line (The Record of Hackensack, 8 January 1969) and a sympathy notice. Her death is given as December 1968 by one index and 6 January 1969 by two others; she was buried on 9 January 1969. The church. Anthony’s side was Maronite, at Our Lady of Lebanon. One Arabic paper of January 1941 says the bride was not Maronite, and the Saydahs used Presbyterian and Episcopal churches (Khaleel studied at a Presbyterian seminary, and Antoon’s funeral was at Christ Episcopal). The December 1940 registers of Our Lady of Lebanon and St. Anselm’s, and Holy Trinity Church’s 1912 register, may say more. The end of Antoon’s life. His South Carolina death certificate and the Eagle name Allendale; two Arabic papers say Columbia. It is probably Allendale; a clearer copy of the certificate would settle it. The church for his funeral is Christ Episcopal in two papers and a street near “76th Street and Fourth Avenue” in the third. His burial is given as Monday 21 November 1949 by one paper and 11 February 1950 by Green-Wood (perhaps a vault). We have not asked Green-Wood for the full records for Antoon and Wassela, and we have no will or estate file. The Tuxedo Park accident, 1916. The papers disagree on whose car it was, who was driving (Antoon or Khaleel) and whether the others were hurt. We do not know how the new trial ordered in December 1918 ended (the last mention is a January 1919 court calendar), and we have not found Najib Maloof’s death certificate (his age at death is 50, 51 or 52 depending on the paper), the court file, or the names of the other men in the car. Antoon’s brothers. Khaleel and Michael say they arrived in 1891, before Ellis Island opened, so the Ellis Island database will not have them. No village register for Forzul is in any collection we use, and the Ottoman population registers have not been searched for the family. Khaleel’s birth. Records give 19 March 1870 (his death certificate), March 1868, about 1867, about 1870, 15 March 1866 and 19 March 1867 (his passport applications). His Beirut degree is dated 1887 by one paper and 1888 by two other sources. Khaleel’s arrival. He says 1891; one 1915 age points to about 1903. The certificate’s 47 years points to about 1901 for New York, but he was at 73 Washington Street in 1900. His Cook County naturalization of 2 November 1896 is known from his own statements and an index card; the petition and certificate have not been seen. We have not found a will or estate file, or Green-Wood’s full records (he appears twice, 29 November 1948 and 1 October 1949). Khaleel’s wife and son. We know Katherine’s family name only as Kourani or Kourany (probably). Her age is 40 on the 1915 census but about 32 on three other records (1882 to 1883). Edward’s birth certificate (Brooklyn, about August 1906) has not been ordered. Michael’s birth and arrival. His own records say 6 August 1877; his sons’ certificates imply about 1869 to 1870. He says he sailed in October 1891, but the 1925 census gives about 1889 for his years in the U.S. We cannot show when he moved from Chicago to Brooklyn: he was there by September 1918 (his draft card). Michael’s naturalization. His own statements say Cook County, 18 March 1903; the 1925 census says Brooklyn, 1915. We have not seen the certificate. Michael’s marriages. We do not know what became of his first wife, Marie Luckey (Grundy County, Illinois, 1901; only an index line is in hand). The Arabic press puts his marriage to Zakeya in Chicago on 5 February 1909, but we have no record of it. Her age is 28 or 32 in 1909 and 1913 (about 1881) and 34 in 1925 (about 1891); her death record (Green-Wood burial, 26 February 1966) should settle it. Michael’s children. His first son’s first name is Jameel on the Cook County birth entry and the 1925 census and James on the 1916 consular certificate. Which did he use? We also lack cemetery records for his infant sons Victor (1919) and Theodore (1922; Mount Olivet), and a death record for his infant daughter Samura (1912), known from an index line. Michael in 1953. His 1953 notices give 8646 Fort Hamilton Parkway, probably a later address than the 8726 of 1922 to 1925. We do not have his death certificate (1 March 1953) or Green-Wood’s full record. Who one bridesmaid at a 1951 wedding was is a question for the family. Murad Saydah. We have no record of when or where Murad died, only that he was alive in January 1920 and his widow Tirkman was widowed by 1929. The 1920 census puts a Murad Saydah, 48, at a jewelry store in Oak Park, and also a Murad Sayyidah, 48, at the Chicago State Hospital four days later; whether they are one man is open. His naturalization is an index card of 19 March 1895 against “about 1897” in his son Harold’s papers. Arrival years for Murad and Tirkman. Murad’s arrival is about February 1890 in one paper, 1886 as we read the 1920 census, and 1891 in his son Ferris’s 1919 registration. Tirkman’s years in the U.S. are 35 in 1925 and 37 in 1929. Tirkman. Her family name is written many ways (Bouinain, Bouman, Abu Aynin and others). Her age at death is 61 or 51 (48 on the 1925 census), and the day of her funeral is Tuesday 10 September 1929 in the Arabic notice and “to-morrow” in the Brooklyn Daily Times of that day. We do not know when she returned from Syria in 1927 or 1928, or who signed Nora’s 1920 papers. Ferris and Fares. Ferris’s birth day is 2 or 26 February 1896, his 1925 census age is a year off both, and his death is placed at Presbyterian Hospital, Manhattan, on the certificate and in Tenafly in an Arabic notice (the certificate is probably right). The wedding of Fares and Alice is 18 December 1926 on the certificate and 11 December in the Arabic notice. His sworn 1919 application says 2 February 1896, so that is probably right; his 1921 and 1923 passport applications may confirm it. Sada and Nustas Kirkish. The 1948, 1949 and 1953 notices name them as Antoon’s sisters. Sada is probably “Sady,” wife of Abdalla Kirkish, in whose Michigan household Antoon boarded in 1900. We have not found a record naming their parents. Her husband is called Abdalo, Assad, Abdalla and Abdullah in different records (probably two men); Nustas’s is “Marun,” Michael and Mike. The 1953 notice says only “California” for both sisters. Sada’s Michigan death record, and the Kirkish naturalization and death records for Marquette County, might settle these. Sada’s and Nustas’s birth years. Sada’s birth is 1874 or 1875 in the census and the California death index, but 14 May 1880 in a Social Security line that may be a different Sadie. Nustas’s is 17 June 1884 in the Social Security index and about 1885 to 1887 in other records. Mary Abraham. In 1920 she is the Kirkish head’s mother-in-law, but Antoon’s mother was Noor. She may be misrecorded, a step-relation, or the Sadie in that household may be someone else. Her own age differs by five years between 1900 and 1920. A question for the family. The Kirkish children. Naseem’s birth is 1899 in Michigan (a birth return of 14 October 1899; the 1900 census says December); a 1922 marriage record that says “born Syria” is probably a different Naseeb. Richard’s middle name is Elias on his birth certificate and John on his death certificate (one boy, probably). The 1920 Forsyth census page reads “Sada” for the wife of a Mikel Kirkish, but the sons are Nustas’s, so she is probably Nustas under a wrong first name. Sada’s immigration year is 1891 in 1900 and 1897 in the 1920 Munising census; a 1912 entry is probably a different Sadie. Evelyn, Virginia and Eli. The 1940 census sheet we found lists only Antoon, Wassela and Helen. Virginia’s marriage to George Hakim is known from newspapers and indexes (on 6 May 1945, though one paper’s “next Sunday” would give 29 April) and Evelyn’s marriages (1953 and 1971 licenses) from indexes. None of the certificates has been ordered, and we do not know where Eli Zrake is buried or who his first wife was beyond the Arabic press of October 1945. Eli’s age at death is 38 or 39. Virginia’s and Evelyn’s births. Virginia’s birth is 29 June 1921 in her index line and about December 1921 by the 1930 census. Evelyn’s 1920 index line spells the family name “Saydak”. Their birth certificates have not been ordered, and we have not shown that “Evelyn Z. Deschner” in Green-Wood’s index is Evelyn Saydah. The Zrake family. Matilda Zrake’s birth is 20 January 1901, 20 November 1901 or 1900, and her first initial is N in one 1962 notice. Green-Wood lists a Matilda buried in December 1954, but several later prints treat her as living. We do not know when Najeeb Zrake died, between 1944 and October 1945, or whether he made a 1914 declaration of intention in Norwich, Connecticut. George Hakim. A 1956 Caravan calls George Hakim the brother of “Mrs. Anthony Awn”; our records make him Virginia’s husband, so Helen’s brother-in-law. No record explains it. A native reader should also check the Arabic engagement, wedding and birth notices for the Hakim and Zuraiq families. The Hadad (Hodod) and Shehadi families The 1892 arrival. We have not found the arrival record for John (Hanna) Hadad, Amina and the children. The censuses give 1892 for the Hadad family; Wassela’s own entries give 1893 and 1895. Hanna Hadad’s birth, death and burial. His birth year is about 1845 on three records and 1850 on the 1900 census. Syracuse papers and an Arabic notice say he died at Clifton Springs; the state death index says Willard (certificate 50442). One paper says he was buried at Morningside Cemetery and Find a Grave says Oakwood Cemetery, Syracuse, with no marker. One paper says eighteen months at Clifton Springs, another eight. His death certificate and the cemetery records would settle these. The Shehadis. Were they Hanna’s brothers-in-law or cousins? Two papers say brothers-in-law and one says cousins (probably brothers-in-law). One Arabic notice names a son-in-law Antoon; another names “Amin Sayda” as the daughter’s husband. Joseph J. Shehadi’s arrival is given as 1892, 1894 or 1897, and his wife Nabeha’s as 1906 or 1908. Frederick Shehadi’s age (13 months in 1907, about five in 1909) cannot be squared yet. Wassela’s brothers and other Haddad men. Salim Hadad’s age is 26 on a 1913 notice but 28 or 29 by the 1900 census; his World War I draft card has not been found. A Najib Haddad buried in Syracuse (1895 to 1955) has two different birth dates, neither matching the 1900 census (October 1896); his Oakwood burial record and Watertown death certificate may show whether he is ours. We do not know where Charles Haddad was in 1900, or what became of Beshara Shahady’s family. Who the Najeeb Hadad of 4721 Sixth Avenue (died 13 January 1914) was is also open. The Hadads’ 1897 arrival sheet. It reads “98 Washington Street”; the Ellis Island index card reads “89” (faint). Helen Hadad and Lily. Helen Hadad’s death date is 21 April 1908 on her certificate and 12 April in an Arabic paper. Mount Olivet’s lot records may show whether she and Lily (1913) share a lot, and who bought it. People at the 1912 wedding. Who “R. G. Haddad” (the physician on Lily’s certificate) and Maheeba Fuleihan (a witness) were, and whether they were relatives, is a question for the family. The Merhige family Amin and Helen Merhige. Amin’s landing is about 1893 on his declaration, about 1901 on a 1941 index and 1900 on the 1930 census. Helen’s years in the U.S. are 1895, 1900 and 1913 in different records, though she is already in the 1905 and 1910 censuses. Georgette’s birth (10 January 1910 by her petition) clashes with her census ages and with when she says she married. We have no burial place for Amin, no death certificates for Amin, Habib or Georgette, and no burial place for the infants. The Merhige connection. A 1897 sheet shows two Hadads going to a “cousin Amin” at the address where Amin Merhige’s brothers were headed. It does not settle whether this Wassilah is Wassela. A question for the family. The 11th Avenue house. The family says Amin built it. Brooklyn building permits and the Kings County deed index for 8314 11th Avenue should show the builder and the year. Everyone Records we cannot yet read. Several Arabic pages are our own translations. A native Arabic reader should check them, especially the notices for George, the Hakim and Zuraiq families, and Tirkman’s. Living memories. A conversation with family would fill in what no record keeps.

Joseph's death certificate, 14 September 1932. The New York City certificate for "Joseph K. Owen," died at about 1 a.m. on 14 September 1932 in Brooklyn, born 21 November 1869, aged 62 years, 9 months, 7 days (this day count does not fit the printed birth date: from 21 November 1869 to 14 September 1932 is 62 years, 9 months and 24 days, while 9 months and 7 days would point to about 7 December 1869, so the records disagree and his birth date is an open question). It lists him as married to "Assin Owen," retired, 12 years in the U.S. and in New York City, son of "Peter Owen" and "Teresa Owen," both of Syria. The cause is cardiac failure (one day), with coronary thrombosis (six days) contributing, signed by the attending physician. Burial was at St. John's Cemetery on 16 September, with Jere J. Cronin, Inc., of 115 Atlantic Avenue as undertaker. The second picture is the bottom of the back of the certificate, where the undertaker's statement is signed "Mrs. Assin Owen" as the "Wife" of the deceased, the person who asked for the burial permit. The record shows the first name Joseph and the family name spelled Owen. Source: New York City Department of Health, Standard Certificate of Death, Brooklyn, registered no. 18405 (1932), as viewed on FamilySearch / New York City Municipal Deaths. Name as written: Joseph K. Owen.

Her date of birth is blank. The cause is acute gangrenous appendicitis (ruptured), after an appendectomy, with toxic myocarditis contributing. She was buried at St. John's Cemetery on 18 October. The back carries the undertaker's statement, which names "John Owen" of 1047 75th Street as her "Son," the next of kin who asked for the burial permit. The record spells the family name Owen. Joseph's death notice, September 1932. As printed: Joseph K. Owen, 62, of 590 78th Street, died "yesterday" at home. He was born in Damour, Syria, and had lived in Brooklyn for 12 years. He leaves his wife, Affin (Assin); four sons, John, Mitchell, Louis and Anthony; and two daughters, Matilda and Theresa. The funeral was to go from the home to St. Mary's Syrian R. C. Church on Hicks Street for a requiem mass, with burial at St. John's Cemetery under J. J. Cronin. Four things stand out. Louis is Elias, who signed his 1937 marriage certificate as Louis J. Awn. The same four sons are named in Esther Ayoub’s 1961 notice. George is named in none of the three notices, and neither is Nassib (Nessil), who died in 1924; we now know why. George drowned in July 1930, as the Arabic papers of that week report, and Nassib died in 1924. The address, 590 78th Street, is also the address on Joseph's death certificate (Document 82), while the 1930 Arabic notice for George (Document 135) gives 466 78th Street. And the funeral church is St. Mary’s Syrian Roman Catholic, while the Arabic papers say Our Lady of Lebanon, so that detail is still open. Source: Brooklyn Times Union, 15 September 1932, page 22 (taken from the file name of the saved copy; the clipping itself does not print the paper or date). Names as printed: Joseph K. Owen, Affin, John, Mitchell, Louis, Anthony, Matilda, Theresa.

Assin's death notice, October 1935. As printed: Assin Owen, 52, a native of Syria, died "yesterday" at her home, 1047 75th Street.
